observations.content:
Summary: The speed of light in vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 m/s, as defined by the International System of Units (SI). This exact value is a result of the redefinition of the metre in 1983, where the metre is now defined as the distance light travels in vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. This definition makes the speed of light a constant and the metre a derived unit.

### Relativity [...] ### Relativity

The speed of light in vacuum is constant, regardless of the motion of the source or the inertial reference frame of the observer.

### Speed

The speed of light in vacuum, c, forms the basis for the definition of the unit of speed, the metre per second.

The fixed numerical value of the speed of light in vacuum, c, is defined exactly:

c \mspace{4mu} = 299 \mspace{4mu} 792 \mspace{4mu} 458 \ \text{m} \ \text{s}^{-1} [...] Inverting this relation gives an exact expression for the metre per second in terms of the speed of light in vacuum, c :

1 \mspace{4mu} \text{m} \mspace{4mu} \text{s}^{-1} \mspace{4mu} = \dfrac{1}{299 \mspace{4mu} 792 \mspace{4mu} 458} \mspace{4mu} c\\  

### Length or distance

The speed of light in vacuum, c, together with the hyperfine transition frequency of the caesium 133 atom, ΔνCs, forms the basis for the definition of the unit of length, the metre.

args.query: CODATA exact speed of light 299792458 metres per second definition

observations.content:
Summary: The CODATA exact speed of light is 299,792,458 metres per second. This value is exact because, by international agreement, a metre is defined as the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 second. The constant c is defined in the International System of Units (SI) as exactly 299,792,458 m/s, used to define the metre as exactly the distance that light travels in vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. This fixed value is used to define the metre, and the second is defined to be the length of time occupied by 9,192,631,770 cycles of the radiation emitted by a caesium-133 atom in a transition between two specified energy states.
